0.title: The Means of Grace and the Growth of the Soul
0.essay:
Spiritual disciplines are not a way to earn God’s favour. They are the means by which we place ourselves before the God who transforms us. That distinction changes everything.

Why we practise them

Someone who prays, reads Scripture, fasts and serves in order to pile up merit has misunderstood both the disciplines and the gospel. Someone who does these things because they long to know God, and because God has promised to meet his people in them, is living the life of grace the disciplines are meant to sustain.

Donald Whitney, in Spiritual Disciplines for the Christian Life, describes them as the God-given means by which we “train” ourselves “for godliness” (1 Timothy 4:7). They are not the goal; Christlikeness is. But just as an athlete who wants to run a marathon trains systematically, the Christian who wants to love God and neighbour freely trains through the disciplines. Jerry Bridges makes the same point in The Practice of Godliness: devotion to God produces the godly character the disciplines aim at, and discipline without devotion is mere religiosity.

Means of grace

The Reformed tradition has always called these practices means of grace: the ordinary channels through which God gives his grace to his people. The Westminster Catechisms name the word, the sacraments and prayer as the chief means; the wider tradition adds fasting, solitude, service, generosity and gathered worship. None of them dispenses grace automatically. But God has promised to use them, and the Christian who neglects them is neglecting the channels through which the river flows.

The chapters

The Foundation — training for godliness; Scripture — feeding on the word; Prayer — the conversation with God; Fasting and Solitude — disciplines of abstinence; Community and Service — disciplines of engagement; and Worship and the Lord’s Supper — the gathered means of grace.

1.title: The Foundation: Training for Godliness
1.essay:
“Rather train yourself for godliness; for while bodily training is of some value, godliness is of value in every way, as it holds promise for the present life and also for the life to come” (1 Timothy 4:7–8).

The gymnasium of the soul

Paul’s word for “train” gives us the English word gymnasium. Godliness does not arrive fully formed; it develops through training. That does not make it self-generated. It is always the fruit of the Spirit. But the Spirit works through the trained, prepared soul, and does so more consistently. Paul does not despise bodily training; it has some value. He calibrates its worth. Godliness holds promise for every part of life, in this age and the next. It is not stumbled into; it is trained toward, through steady practice the Spirit uses to form Christ in us.

Two dangers

On one side lies legalism: treating the disciplines as works that earn credit with God, or as the condition of his love. Whoever prays in order to be worthy of God’s attention has misunderstood the gospel. On the other side lies passivity: believing that because God is sovereign and grace is free, effort is irrelevant and the disciplines are a kind of works-righteousness.

The New Testament charts a third way: “work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:12–13). Our effort and God’s working are not rivals; they run together. The disciplines are the form “working out” takes — the deliberate, embodied practices through which the soul cooperates with what God is doing. “Fear and trembling” is not the anxiety of someone unsure of God’s acceptance, but the reverence of someone who knows they are working alongside the living God.

Placing ourselves in the path of grace

The disciplines train the whole person — body, mind, will and affections — toward God. They do not transform us directly; they place us in the path of God’s transforming grace. A simple picture helps: we cannot produce a sunrise, but we can be in the right place to see it.

So they are always practised in the context of grace already received, never in order to get it. The Christian who reads Scripture does so as a child reading a letter from their Father, not a student earning a grade. The Christian who fasts does so as one whose deepest hunger Christ has already satisfied, not as one trying to attract God’s attention by suffering. The motive changes everything.

The cost and the fruit

“For the moment all discipline seems painful rather than pleasant, but later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it” (Hebrews 12:11). That is the logic of all training. The discomfort of rising early to pray, the flesh’s resistance to fasting, the busyness that makes solitude feel irresponsible — these are the costs. The fruit, a soul increasingly at peace with God and formed in righteousness, comes to those who have been trained by it. Not those who have read about it; those trained by it.

“Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind” (Romans 12:2). The world constantly presses its patterns on us — its values, anxieties and definitions of success. The disciplines are the counter-pressure: the daily, deliberate turning of the mind back toward God, his word and his kingdom. A transformed mind is not achieved overnight; it is renewed day by day.

Abstinence and engagement

Richard Foster divides the disciplines into inward (meditation, prayer, fasting, study), outward (simplicity, solitude, submission, service) and corporate (confession, worship, guidance, celebration). Dallas Willard distinguishes disciplines of abstinence — fasting, solitude, silence, frugality — from disciplines of engagement — study, worship, prayer, service. We need both. Abstinence makes space; engagement fills it with God.

Be killing sin

John Owen’s The Mortification of Sin is among the most searching works on the discipline of putting sin to death. Its central maxim is famous: “Be killing sin, or it will be killing you.” Owen grounded it firmly in the Spirit’s work — “if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live” (Romans 8:13) — while insisting on the believer’s active cooperation. Spiritual discipline is always Spirit-empowered human effort, never one without the other.

The Puritans also practised regular family worship — morning and evening prayer, Scripture reading and psalm-singing — as the household form of the means of grace. Richard Baxter urged ministers to visit and catechise every family, convinced that the church is renewed as homes are renewed. A family practising the disciplines together is doing church at the kitchen table.

For reflection

Are you more prone to legalism or passivity about spiritual disciplines? What would it look like to practise them as a child receiving a letter rather than a student earning a grade? Which discipline do you most need to “train” in this season?

2.title: Scripture: Feeding on the Word
2.essay:
The first and most fundamental discipline is the reading, study and meditation of Scripture. Everything else in the Christian life depends on it, because the word is the chief instrument through which God speaks, the Spirit illuminates, and faith is sustained. Without Scripture, every other discipline drifts from its source.

Reading, study and meditation

The discipline works at three levels. Reading is the regular, systematic movement through the text, giving a whole-Bible perspective. Study is the careful examination of a passage — its grammar, context and meaning. Meditation is the slow turning of a text over in the mind, letting it move from the intellect to the heart and will, so that it shapes what we feel, want and do.

A tree by the water

The blessed person delights in the law of the Lord, “and on his law he meditates day and night. He is like a tree planted by streams of water that yields its fruit in its season, and its leaf does not wither” (Psalm 1:2–3). Not a tree that occasionally visits the stream, but one whose roots are always in the water. Its fruit is not the result of its effort but of its position. The fruit comes in its season — not always at once, not always visibly — but it comes, because the root is in the word.

The Hebrew word for meditate is used elsewhere of a lion growling over its prey and of a dove cooing: both pictures of absorbed, sustained attention. Meditation in Scripture is not emptying the mind but filling it with God’s word and staying with it until it does its work.

Meditate, so that you may do

God told Joshua, “This Book of the Law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, so that you may be careful to do according to all that is written in it” (Joshua 1:8). Meditation is not an end in itself. It is the way the word moves from the mind to the will and then to action. The prosperity promised there is not chiefly material; it is the flourishing of a life aligned with God’s instruction.

Scripture is profitable “for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness” (2 Timothy 3:16). It forms the mind with truth, exposes what is wrong, redirects toward what is right and builds the habits of a godly life. Submitting to it in all four ways forms us “for every good work”. It is not one practice among many but the one that makes the others coherent.

Open my eyes

“Open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law” (Psalm 119:18). This is the prayer for the start of every reading. The wondrous things are already there; our eyes need opening. It is a prayer of dependence — I cannot see without you — and of expectation — there is treasure to find. The Reformers insisted that word and Spirit belong together. Word without Spirit becomes dead orthodoxy; Spirit without word becomes subjective impressionism. The Spirit who inspired Scripture also illuminates it.

The ancient practice of lectio divina, sacred reading — reading slowly, noticing a word or phrase that arrests you, sitting with it in prayer, and letting it move from mind to will — has been practised since Benedict. Reformed Christians have sometimes suspected it as too mystical, but its instinct is sound: Scripture is to be received, not merely processed. “The word of God is living and active” (Hebrews 4:12), and whoever reads it as a living letter from the living God will read differently from someone handling a textbook.

Stored in the heart

“I have stored up your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you” (Psalm 119:11). The memorised word is the word that is there in the moment of temptation, grief or decision, when there is no time to look anything up. Whoever has filled their memory with Scripture has given the Spirit a vast vocabulary to use in their hardest moments. Memorisation is among the most underrated and fruitful disciplines there is.

Müller and M’Cheyne

For decades George Müller fed his soul on Scripture before anything else each day. He would read until a verse or passage arrested him, meditate on it, and then pray it back to God. That pattern — Scripture leading to meditation leading to prayer — was, he said, the foundation of his whole life of faith. The first business of the morning must be the soul’s nourishment, not the day’s tasks.

Robert Murray M’Cheyne’s reading plan of 1842, which takes the reader through the Old Testament once and the New Testament and Psalms twice in a year, has fed countless Christians for nearly two centuries. A plan is not legalism; it is structure serving breadth. Someone who reads only favourite passages has a diet as unbalanced as someone who eats one food. The whole counsel of God needs the whole Bible.

For reflection

Which of the three — reading, study or meditation — is weakest in your life? Pray Psalm 119:18 before you next open your Bible. Choose one verse to memorise this week. Would a reading plan help you take in the whole counsel of God?

3.title: Prayer: The Conversation with God
3.essay:
Prayer is the most essential and the most neglected discipline of the Christian life. Essential, because it is the creature’s daily conversation with the Creator, in which the soul returns to the God it came from and is going to. Neglected, because it is hard: it demands a disciplined mind, a humbled will and a patience the world has trained out of us.

The map Jesus gave

The Lord’s Prayer (Matthew 6:9–13) is the template Jesus gave. It has an address (“Our Father in heaven”), adoration (“hallowed be your name”), submission (“your kingdom come, your will be done”), petition (“give us this day our daily bread”), confession (“forgive us our debts”) and protection (“lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil”), and the church has long added the doxology, “for yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory”. It is not a script to recite but a map of the ground genuine prayer covers. Prayer shaped by it is comprehensive, not just a list of requests.

Notice that it begins with two priorities before any petition: God’s name and God’s kingdom. Before we ask for anything for ourselves, we align ourselves with his glory and purposes. That reorders the whole motive of prayer — not “Here are my needs; please meet them,” but “Here is your glory; I align myself with it, and from there I bring my needs.” As we pray it, we are shaped into people whose first concern is God’s honour rather than our comfort.

Without ceasing

“Pray without ceasing” (1 Thessalonians 5:17) does not mean spending twenty-four hours on our knees. It means a continuous turning of the heart toward God: the brief prayer in a traffic jam, the whispered thanks over a meal, the moment of intercession when a name comes to mind, the habit of returning our attention to God through the day. The tradition calls this practising the presence of God.

Brother Lawrence, a seventeenth-century Carmelite lay brother, practised prayer as an unbroken conversation with God through every moment, including washing dishes in the monastery kitchen. His The Practice of the Presence of God describes a soul that has learned to live aware of God. That is Paul’s command made flesh: not a programme but a posture.

Prayer instead of anxiety

“Do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 4:6–7). The alternative to anxiety is not solving the problem but praying. Paul does not promise that God will fix the situation; he promises that God’s peace will stand guard over the heart. The peace comes not from answered petitions but from the praying itself. It surpasses understanding because it does not depend on circumstances improving.

Do not lose heart

Jesus told the parable of the persistent widow “to the effect that they ought always to pray and not lose heart” (Luke 18:1). The two go together. Persistence in prayer is not an attempt to overcome God’s reluctance; it is the form faith takes when the answer has not yet come.

And when we cannot find words at all, “the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words” (Romans 8:26), according to the will of God. The believer who sits before God unable to form a prayer is not failing at the discipline. They are exactly where the Spirit meets us. Bring the silence, and let the Spirit pray.

Promises and answers

Jesus’ promises about prayer are extraordinary: “Ask, and it will be given to you” (Matthew 7:7); “Whatever you ask in my name, this I will do” (John 14:13); “If you abide in me, and my words abide in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you” (John 15:7). They are not blank cheques but covenant promises, shaped by relationship (abiding in Christ), alignment (asking in his name, in keeping with his character) and faith. God is not a vending machine but a Father who gives good gifts.

Unanswered prayer is a universal experience, and Scripture is honest about it. Sometimes the answer is delayed (Luke 18:1–8); sometimes it is no (2 Corinthians 12:8–9); sometimes it is “far more abundantly than all that we ask or think” (Ephesians 3:20). Prayer includes trusting God’s wisdom in his answers, the faith that says with Job, “Though he slay me, I will hope in him” (Job 13:15).

Intercession

Praying for others — family, friends, colleagues, church members, enemies and the nations — is one of the most powerful forms of love there is. Jesus modelled it in his high-priestly prayer (John 17), and he continues it at the Father’s right hand (Romans 8:34). When we intercede, we share in the intercession of the ascended Christ.

George Müller kept detailed records of his prayers and God’s answers across seventy years. He prayed for specific people, needs and amounts, and God answered specifically. The story is often told that he prayed for decades for the conversion of several friends, some of whom came to faith only after his death. His journals argue that God answers prayer — not always quickly or as expected, but faithfully.

For reflection

Pray slowly through the Lord’s Prayer, letting each line open into your own words. Where could you build small moments of “praying without ceasing” into your day? What anxiety do you need to bring to God with thanksgiving? Whom will you commit to pray for persistently?

4.title: Fasting and Solitude: Disciplines of Abstinence
4.essay:
The disciplines of abstinence — fasting, solitude, silence and simplicity — work by making space. They remove something (food, company, noise, possessions) to expose what it was masking, and to make room for God.

Uncomfortable revelations

Fasting reveals what actually controls us. Solitude reveals who we are when stripped of performance and activity. Silence reveals the noise of our own inner life. Simplicity reveals what we really depend on. These are uncomfortable revelations, and the discomfort is the point.

When you fast

Fasting is the most countercultural discipline in a culture organised around consumption and comfort. Jesus assumes his disciples will fast: “And when you fast, do not look gloomy like the hypocrites” (Matthew 6:16) — when, not if. His instructions concern motive and manner, not frequency. The hypocrites fasted to be seen as spiritual; Jesus says fast invisibly, so that the only audience is the Father. That principle governs all the disciplines. They are practised before God, not for the gallery. A discipline performed for human approval has its reward in that approval, and that is all it will get.

The church has historically fasted regularly: weekly, in seasons such as Lent, or in response to particular needs. Reformed Christians have sometimes neglected fasting as too Catholic or too works-centred, but the biblical case for it is stronger than that dismissal allows.

Fasting is not self-punishment or an attempt to earn God’s attention by suffering. It is hunger turned into prayer: the body’s emptiness declaring the soul’s need and clearing space for God. And it flows into justice. “Is not this the fast that I choose: to loose the bonds of wickedness, to undo the straps of the yoke, to let the oppressed go free, and to break every yoke? Is it not to share your bread with the hungry and bring the homeless poor into your house?” (Isaiah 58:6–7). Someone who fasts and then ignores the hungry has missed the point. The faster’s empty stomach should become the servant’s compassion. Fasting that produces self-righteousness has failed.

He would withdraw

“But he would withdraw to desolate places and pray” (Luke 5:16). The tense describes a habit: repeatedly, regularly. And it comes in the middle of intense public ministry. The busier Jesus became, the more he withdrew. That is counterintuitive for activists: surely the crowd’s needs demand more time in the crowd? Jesus’ pattern says the capacity to serve the crowd is sustained by withdrawing from it. A soul that never retreats into solitude with God is drawing on capital it never replenishes. The desert fathers and mothers made solitude the foundation of their spiritual life. For most of us the problem is not too much solitude but too little; the noise of modern life fills every potential quiet moment.

Solitude also produces self-knowledge. Thomas à Kempis asked what good it does to discuss the Trinity profoundly if we lack humility. Whoever is always in company can always manage their image; whoever is regularly alone with God meets who they really are. That is not pleasant, but it is the ground of real repentance, real dependence and real growth. Henri Nouwen, in The Way of the Heart, called solitude the furnace of transformation, where the false self built for others’ approval is dismantled and the true self grounded in God’s love emerges. He warned that someone who cannot be alone with God cannot truly be with others either; they will use community as an escape from themselves rather than a gift to others.

Be still

“Be still, and know that I am God” (Psalm 46:10). The word means to let go, to sink down, to release. And it is spoken not to people at leisure but to people in crisis, while the nations rage and kingdoms totter (Psalm 46:6). Stillness before God is hardest and most needed when things are most urgent: the deliberate stopping, in the middle of the noise, to know God, not merely facts about him. God spoke to Elijah not in the earthquake or the fire but in “the sound of a low whisper” (1 Kings 19:12). The disciple who cultivates silence can hear what constant noise drowns out. Stillness is the discipline of trust.

Jesus in the wilderness

Before his public ministry began, Jesus fasted forty days in the wilderness (Matthew 4:1–11). The fasting was not the point; the preparation was. Those days of hunger, silence and solitude produced the clarity and strength that withstood Satan’s temptations, and every temptation was met with Scripture absorbed in that solitude. The pattern is instructive. The great works of ministry are usually prepared for in the hidden disciplines.

For reflection

What might fasting reveal about what controls you? Could you set aside one meal this week to pray, and give what it would have cost to someone in need? Where could you find regular solitude, even briefly? What would it mean to “be still” in the middle of your present pressures?

5.title: Community and Service: Disciplines of Engagement
5.essay:
The disciplines of engagement — service, generosity, confession, accountability and community — work in the opposite direction from those of abstinence. Fasting and solitude make space by removing; service and community fill space by engaging. Together they make the full shape of the Christian life.

Both directions

Whoever withdraws to be with God must also engage with neighbours in love, and whoever serves their neighbour must also withdraw to be resourced by God. Neither direction works alone.

Service

“For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). Service is not just a helpful activity; it is the posture of those who follow the Servant-King. Jesus does not merely commend it; he embodies it, and gives that as the reason we should serve. The discipline of service is the discipline of becoming like Jesus — not by aspiring to his divine attributes but by taking his posture toward others: willing to take the lowly place, ready to give rather than accumulate.

Service trains us out of the instinctive self-centredness of the fallen self. It requires putting our preferences under someone else’s need. Whoever washes up after the church event, visits the lonely elderly member or mentors the struggling teenager is doing something to their own soul as well as to their neighbour’s situation. Service done in secret, without recognition, is one of the most potent ways of putting pride to death. The Puritans understood that self-denial must be concrete and habitual, cutting across the grain of the fallen self and training the heart in the self-forgetfulness that marks Christ’s character.

Confession

“Therefore, confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed” (James 5:16). Confession may be the most neglected discipline in Protestant evangelicalism. The Reformation rightly rejected the Roman confessional with its system of priestly absolution, but sometimes wrongly threw out accountable confession with it. Sin carried in secret has a power it would lose in the light. Naming it to a trusted brother or sister, and receiving their prayer and assurance of grace, is humbling, because it destroys the pretence of self-sufficiency. It is also liberating, because it brings the sin into the community of grace where it can be dealt with. The healing James promises is not only physical; it is the healing of a soul that secrecy has been making sick.

John Wesley’s Methodist movement was built on small groups of eight to twelve who met weekly for mutual accountability, confession and prayer. The question put to each member was, “How is it with your soul?” Those class meetings and bands were the engine of the transformation the revival produced. It was not only preached into being; it was sustained by disciplined, accountable community.

Gathering

“And let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works, not neglecting to meet together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another, and all the more as you see the Day drawing near” (Hebrews 10:24–25). The nearness of the Day is a reason to increase commitment to community, not withdraw from it. This is not casual attendance when convenient but a deliberate commitment to a body of believers who know you, challenge you, pray for you and hold you to account. Whoever has that has one of the most powerful means of grace there is; whoever lacks it is vulnerable in ways they may not even recognise. Neglecting regular gathering is not a lifestyle preference but the neglect of a commanded means of grace.

Generosity

Watching people put gifts into the temple treasury, Jesus said, “Truly, I tell you, this poor widow has put in more than all of them. For they all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty put in all she had to live on” (Luke 21:3–4). Generosity is measured not by the amount given but by what is left. Giving that touches our lifestyle is a discipline; giving comfortably from surplus is closer to tax management. The widow’s two coins declared: God is my provision, and what I have is his.

Systematic, proportional giving — the tithe as a starting point, not a ceiling — trains the soul in detachment from money and attachment to the kingdom. Whoever gives regularly and generously is training themselves to believe what they say: that God provides, that the kingdom is their treasure, and that earthly wealth is a trust to be used for eternal purposes, not a security to be hoarded against an uncertain future.

The first church

The earliest church devoted itself to the apostles’ teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread and prayer, and its members sold possessions and distributed to anyone in need (Acts 2:42–47). This was not communism. It was the spontaneous fruit of a community so captivated by the gospel and so loving that the ordinary boundaries of property loosened before a neighbour’s need — the corporate practice of the disciplines producing corporate transformation.

For reflection

What hidden act of service could you do this week, telling no one? Is there someone you trust enough to confess sin to and pray with? How committed are you, really, to a body of believers who know you? What would generosity that touches your lifestyle look like for you?

6.title: Worship and the Lord’s Supper: The Gathered Means of Grace
6.essay:
Corporate worship is not an optional extra to the private disciplines. It is their crown and completion. We are baptised into a body (1 Corinthians 12:13), built together into a dwelling place for God (Ephesians 2:22), made a royal priesthood (1 Peter 2:9). The private disciplines of prayer, Scripture and service find their fullest expression and their ongoing nourishment in the gathered worship of God’s people.

Let us

“Oh come, let us worship and bow down; let us kneel before the LORD, our Maker!” (Psalm 95:6). The psalmist uses the plural throughout. Worship in Scripture is characteristically corporate. The discipline of gathered worship is the discipline of showing up: bringing your whole self to the assembly and bowing with brothers and sisters whose presence corrects the individualism private devotion can breed.

True worshippers worship “in spirit and truth” (John 4:23–24). Spirit: genuine, heartfelt, Spirit-empowered engagement with the living God. Truth: grounded in who God is as Scripture reveals him, not in our preferences or moods. Gathered worship trains both, the heart by repeated practice and the mind by steady exposure to the word.

God’s terms

The Reformed regulative principle — in worship we do what Scripture commands — is not an exercise in minimalism but a commitment to letting God set the terms of his own worship. The elements of a Reformed service — call to worship, confession and assurance of pardon, Scripture reading, psalms and hymns, prayer, sermon, the Lord’s Supper and benediction — are each drawn from Scripture and apostolic practice. Nothing is filler; every element is a means of grace. The Worship and the Lord’s Day study explores this further.

The Supper

The Lord’s Supper is the central act of gathered worship: the meal the risen Christ hosts, in which he feeds his people with himself, and in which the church proclaims his death until he comes. The Reformers disagreed about how Christ is present — Luther held a real bodily presence, Zwingli a memorial, and Calvin a spiritual presence — but they agreed that the Supper is a means of grace, a seal of the covenant and a foretaste of the coming feast.

Calvin argued, against both Lutheran and Zwinglian tendencies, that Christ is truly present in the Supper, but by the Spirit rather than physically in the elements. The Westminster Confession says that worthy receivers “inwardly by faith, really and indeed, yet not carnally and corporally but spiritually, receive, and feed upon, Christ crucified, and all benefits of his death.” The Supper does not merely remind us of Christ’s death; it feeds the soul with the living Christ who died. It seals the promises of the gospel and assures the doubting believer that Christ’s body was given for them.

A proclamation

“For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (1 Corinthians 11:26). The Supper is a declaration as well as a receiving. Each time the church breaks bread and pours wine, it announces to the powers, to the watching world and to its own doubting members that Jesus died, that his death was enough, and that he is coming again. “Until he comes” gives the meal its urgency and hope: it is eaten in the light of the marriage supper of the Lamb.

Coming prepared

“Let a person examine himself, then, and so eat of the bread and drink of the cup” (1 Corinthians 11:28). That examination is not the morbid self-interrogation that drove Luther to exhaustion. It is the honest, hopeful self-examination of a believer who wants to come to the table with real repentance and real faith. The prepared communicant has looked at their heart, confessed their sin and comes hungry for the grace the Supper offers.

It also involves our relationships. Jesus said, “So if you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar and go. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift” (Matthew 5:23–24). The early church exchanged the kiss of peace before the Eucharist, a gesture of reconciliation that made it impossible to receive the Supper while nursing a grudge. Worship that begins with honest confession, includes real reconciliation and culminates in the Supper engages the whole person — mind, conscience, relationships and soul.

Calvin’s longing

Calvin wanted weekly communion in Geneva but was overruled by the city council, which feared the people were not ready. He accepted quarterly communion reluctantly and spent his ministry urging more frequent celebration. He believed the Supper was the gospel made visible and tangible, and that a church which rarely celebrated it was a malnourished church, rarely seeing the gospel enacted. His Short Treatise on the Lord’s Supper remains one of the most accessible and beautiful treatments of its meaning. Frequent, attentive, prepared participation in the Supper is among the most undervalued means of grace in much of evangelicalism.

A rehearsal

“Let us rejoice and exult and give him the glory, for the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his Bride has made herself ready” (Revelation 19:7). Every act of gathered worship is a rehearsal for that moment. A small congregation in an unremarkable building on an ordinary Sunday is, in God’s economy, taking part in something cosmic: the worship of the Creator by his redeemed creatures, a foretaste of the worship that will one day be everything.

For reflection

Do you come to gathered worship as a consumer or a participant? How could you prepare for the next Lord’s Supper? Is there anyone you need to be reconciled with before you come to the table? What would change if you saw each Sunday as a rehearsal for Revelation 19?
